lesson.title: Major Scales and Keys
lesson.summary: One pattern of whole and half steps builds every major scale, and the key signature collects its sharps or flats.

section.title: The major scale pattern
section.p: A scale is a series of notes in order of pitch, from a starting note, the tonic, up to the tonic an octave higher. In major and minor scales each letter is used once before the tonic returns.
The major scale follows this pattern of whole steps (W) and half steps (H):

callout.p: W W H W W W H. The half steps lie between the third and fourth notes and between the seventh and eighth.

section.p: Played on the white keys from C to C, the scale fits the pattern exactly, because the white-key half steps E–F and B–C fall in the right places.

figure.caption: The C major scale. The highlighted pairs are the half steps, 3–4 and 7–8.

section.p: The scale falls into two equal halves of four notes, each with the pattern W W H, joined by a whole step in the middle.

section.title: Building a major scale
section.p: A major scale can start on any note. Write the letters in order, then add sharps or flats until the steps match the pattern.

worked.title: Build a major scale that needs sharps

step.p: Take D as the tonic and write the eight letters from D up to D.

figure.staff: D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5 D5

step.p: Check the steps from the bottom. D–E is a whole step, as required. E–F should be a whole step but is a half step, so raise F to F#. Now F#–G is the half step the pattern needs.
G–A and A–B are whole steps. B–C should be a whole step, so raise C to C#; C#–D is then the final half step.
The D major scale is D E F# G A B C# D.

section.p: Some scales need flats instead. In F major, A–B would be a whole step where the pattern needs a half step, so B is lowered to Bb: F G A Bb C D E F.

figure.staff: F4 G4 A4 *Bb4 C5 D5 E5 F5
figure.caption: The F major scale has one flat.

section.p: A major scale uses either sharps or flats, never both.

check.prompt: Which note needs an accidental in the G major scale?
check.explanation: From G, the letters are G A B C D E F G. E–F must be a whole step and F–G a half step, so F becomes F#. B–C is already the half step needed between the third and fourth notes.

check.prompt: What is the fourth note of the Eb major scale?
check.explanation: Eb–F and F–G are whole steps; the third and fourth notes must be a half step apart, and G–A is a whole step, so the fourth note is Ab.

section.title: Key signatures
section.p: Music in a major key uses the notes of its major scale. Instead of writing the same sharps or flats again and again, they are collected in a key signature at the start of every staff, right after the clef.
A sharp or flat in the key signature applies to every note with that letter, in every octave, until the key signature changes.
Sharps and flats always appear in the same order. A key with two sharps has the first two sharps of the order, a key with five flats the first five flats.

callout.p: Order of sharps: F# C# G# D# A# E# B#.
Order of flats, the same letters backwards: Bb Eb Ab Db Gb Cb Fb.

figure.caption: All seven sharps in the treble and bass clefs.
All seven flats in the treble and bass clefs.

section.p: To name a major key from its signature:

list.li: Sharps: the last sharp is the seventh note of the scale. The tonic is a half step above it.
Flats: the second-to-last flat is the tonic. With a single flat, the key is F major.
No sharps or flats: C major.

worked.title: Name the major key with four sharps

step.p: Take the first four sharps of the order: F# C# G# D#.
The last one, D#, is the seventh note of the scale.
A half step above D#, on the next letter, is E. The key is E major.

check.prompt: Which major key has this key signature?

figure.description: A treble staff with a key signature of three flats.

check.explanation: The three flats are Bb, Eb and Ab. The second-to-last flat, Eb, names the key. The last flat, Ab, is the fourth note of the scale.

check.prompt: Which major key has two sharps?
check.explanation: The two sharps are F# and C#. The last sharp, C#, is the seventh note, and a half step above it is D. G major has only F#.

section.title: The circle of fifths
section.p: A fifth is the distance from one note to the fifth letter above it, counting both: from C up to G is a fifth. The intervals lesson explains it fully.

Start on C major and go up a fifth at a time: each new key has one more sharp. Go down a fifth at a time instead, and each new key has one more flat. Arranged in a circle like the hours of a clock, with C at the top, the keys form the circle of fifths.

list.li: Sharp keys, going up in fifths: G (1), D (2), A (3), E (4), B (5), F# (6), C# (7).
Flat keys, going down in fifths: F (1), Bb (2), Eb (3), Ab (4), Db (5), Gb (6), Cb (7).

section.p: The new sharp in each sharp key is its seventh note, and the new flat in each flat key is its fourth note.

At the bottom of the circle the two sides overlap. Three pairs of keys sound the same but are written differently: B major (5 sharps) and Cb major (7 flats), F# major (6 sharps) and Gb major (6 flats), C# major (7 sharps) and Db major (5 flats). These are enharmonic keys. Counting C, there are fifteen major key signatures.

check.prompt: How many sharps does A major have?
check.explanation: Going up in fifths from C: G has one sharp, D two, A three: F#, C# and G#.

check.prompt: Which major key has six flats?
check.explanation: The six flats end with Gb and Cb; the second-to-last, Gb, is the tonic. Db major has five flats and Cb major seven.
